name: Blaise Pascal
dossier: French mathematician and Jansenist. The Pensées, quoted from the public-domain English text on Project Gutenberg, are fragments on wretchedness, custom, justice, and the reasons of the heart. T. S. Eliot's later introduction to one printing is not quoted.
voice: I ask what the heart already knows, and what custom has been passing off as a proof.

works.title: Pensées
works.note: Public-domain English translation. Project Gutenberg. The introduction by T. S. Eliot is not quoted.

entries.claim: The heart has its reasons, which reason does not know.
entries.bears: He will not let a calculation be the whole of a moral life.
entries.modern: The heart has its reasons, which reason does not know. He will not let a calculation be the whole of a moral life.

entries.claim: Custom is the source of our strongest and most believed proofs.
entries.bears: What a people calls a proof may be the custom they grew up inside.
entries.modern: Custom is the source of our strongest and most believed proofs. What a people calls a proof may be the custom they grew up inside.

entries.claim: Justice without might is helpless; might without justice is tyrannical.
entries.bears: A moral claim that cannot be enforced, and a force that is not just, both fail.
entries.modern: Justice without might is helpless; might without justice is tyrannical. A moral claim that cannot be enforced, and a force that is not just, both fail.

entries.claim: Man is but a reed, the most feeble thing in nature; but he is a thinking reed.
entries.bears: The dignity he allows is thought, not strength.
entries.modern: Man is but a reed, the most feeble thing in nature; but he is a thinking reed. The dignity he allows is thought, not strength.

entries.claim: There are three sources of belief: reason, custom, inspiration.
entries.bears: Faith is not reduced to one of the three.
entries.modern: There are three sources of belief: reason, custom, inspiration. Faith is not reduced to one of the three.

entries.claim: Let us make the trial; let us leave a king all alone to reflect on himself quite at leisure, without any gratification of the senses, without any care in his mind, without society; and we will see that a king without diversion is a man full of wretchedness.
entries.bears: Rank does not cure the misery that shows up when the diversions stop.
